abstract: |
  Climate finance pays countries for marginal emission cuts measured against counterfactuals nobody can observe, and pays almost nothing for carbon stocks never released. This paper proposes a notional capitalized value: a balance opened by a country's carbon stock, debited for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance, and used not as cash but as guarantee capacity on its green borrowing. A guarantee saves the borrower the full credit spread but costs its provider only expected loss and the carry on a buffer, so each dollar of donor cost delivers about 2.7 dollars of incentive in a conservative base case and far more on the development banks' own sovereign loss record. The stock should set the size of the balance and a separate price the debit per tonne. For a stylized forest country with Guyana's carbon stock, a $5 billion balance saves $150 million a year and prices emissions at about $30 per tonne, at a donor cost near $11. Capacity that declines as fast as technology costs fall is the cheapest way to make acting now beat waiting.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Guyana keeps about 19.5 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent in some 18 million hectares of forest [@Guyana2022LCDS]. At the $20 per tonne that Hess agreed to pay for Guyana's forest credits, that stock would be worth $390 billion. Guyana is paid for none of it. What it sells is the gap between its actual deforestation and a reference level: 33.47 million credits for 2016–2020 [@OilNow2022], of which 37.5 million over 2016–2030 go to Hess for at least $750 million [@GuyanaDPI2023], about $50 million a year. The same rules pay a country that clears forest and replants, and pay a high-deforestation country for slowing down, but they pay little or nothing to one that never cleared. Leaving coal or oil in the ground earns nothing at all.

Two defects follow, and both are about the form of the reward rather than its size. First, paying for marginal tonnes against a counterfactual rewards whoever can claim the most generous baseline, and studies of project-based forest offsets find that baselines were routinely inflated [@West2023]. Second, the payment arrives after the result, often years after a government pays the political cost of reform, so it guards against reversal more than it starts anything [@Angelsen2017; @StrettonTC, ch. 20]. Neither defect is fixed by paying more per tonne, and donors will not in any case vote for cash transfers on the scale that the carbon stocks of tropical forest countries would justify.

This paper asks how the international system can give a government a large, early and credible incentive to protect carbon stocks and cut emissions, without a cash transfer that donors will not vote for.

The answer is to credit each participating country with a notional capitalized value (NCV): an opening balance set by its carbon stock, debited for every tonne it emits above an agreed allowance and credited for every tonne below it. The balance is never paid out. It sets the country's guarantee capacity, the maximum outstanding guarantee exposure that multilateral development banks (MDBs), backed by a buffer fund, will provide on the country's eligible green borrowing. The country gains the spread it saves on guaranteed debt; donors bear the expected loss on the exposure and the carry cost of the buffer. Because each tonne emitted shrinks the balance, the incentive acts from the first year. Because capacity can be scheduled to decline, the reward is largest for acting early.

The paper makes four contributions.

1. **It reconciles four formulations** of the idea found in earlier drafts (interest on a notional value, guarantee capacity, a climate balance on stocks and long-run emissions, and a "climate allowance" of guarantee capacity), and chooses guarantee capacity as the main form, with interest on the balance paid into a trust account as a variant for countries that do not borrow (@sec-definition).
2. **It derives what the incentive is worth and what it costs** (@sec-model). The ratio of incentive value to guarantor cost equals the spread saved divided by expected loss plus buffer carry (Proposition 1). It is 2.7 in the series' conservative base case, in which governments fail to honor 3 percent of guarantee obligations a year and lose creditors 37 cents on the dollar, and about 80 on the MDBs' own sovereign loss record. The debit must be per tonne emitted and the capacity must bind, or the marginal incentive is zero; when both hold, the incentive is equivalent to a carbon price equal to the debit price times the spread over the discount rate (Proposition 2). Acting now beats waiting if and only if the initial incentive per tonne covers the interest and technology-cost return to waiting, and the cheapest schedule that achieves this lets capacity decline at the rate technology costs fall (Proposition 3).
3. **It separates the two prices.** A single notional price cannot do both jobs. Priced high enough to bite at the margin, Guyana's stock is worth $1.95 trillion at $100 per tonne, which no guarantor can stand behind; priced low enough to fit the country's borrowing, the margin is worth $0.15 per tonne. The stock should set the size of the balance and a separate debit price should set the reward per tonne. The stock is what makes the debit possible: a negative transfer to a sovereign is unenforceable, but a deduction from a balance it has not yet drawn is not.
4. **It calibrates the scheme** for a forest country with Guyana's verified stock, for a coal-reserve country with Indonesia's reserves, and for the scale needed to make an incentive big (@sec-calibration). It corrects the arithmetic of the original proposal, which understates the incentive tenfold under the most natural reading.

The closest work is the conservation-contract literature, which shows that paying a resource owner to conserve a stock can beat demand-side policy when the owner would otherwise sell [@Harstad2016; @Harstad2012], and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, which pays forest countries per hectare of standing forest out of the spread on a leveraged bond portfolio [@Barber2025]. This paper differs from both in delivering the reward through guarantees, where the gap between the borrower's value and the provider's cost creates the leverage, and in deriving the conditions under which the reward changes what a government does and when.

# Literature and precedents {#sec-literature}

*Results-based forest finance pays for flows against reference levels.* The Paris Agreement encourages results-based payments for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD+) [@UNFCCC2015, Article 5.2]. Norway's bilateral agreements with Brazil, Guyana, Indonesia and Tanzania, the largest such programs, were only partly performance-based, and a review of them identifies reference levels, performance criteria, risk sharing and the credibility of funding as the main design problems of results-based aid [@Angelsen2017]. Jurisdictional standards such as ART-TREES moved crediting from projects to national or subnational territories, which removes within-country leakage and makes the counterfactual a national rather than a project baseline. Guyana is the leading case: ART issued it 33.47 million credits for 2016–2020 in December 2022 [@OilNow2022], and Hess agreed to buy 37.5 million credits to 2030 for at least $750 million, starting at $15 per tonne for the 2016 and 2017 vintages [@GuyanaDPI2023]. The price is modest, the stream is long, and the payment is for avoided flow, not for the stock.

*Baselines are the weak point.* A synthetic-control study of voluntary forest-conservation projects found that most claimed reductions far exceeded any measurable effect, because baselines were set above what would have happened [@West2023]. Jurisdictional baselines are harder to game but face the same logic: a country whose deforestation was always low has little to sell, and a country that raised deforestation before the baseline period is rewarded for lowering it again. This is the additionality problem at the level of states, and it pays for waiting [@StrettonTC, ch. 20].

*Stock-based payments exist but are small.* The Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), launched by Brazil on 6 November 2025 with the World Bank as trustee and interim host, aims to raise $25 billion of junior sponsor capital, lent for 40 years at rates comparable to US Treasury yields, and about $100 billion from market investors, for $125 billion in all [@Barber2025]. It invests in emerging-market bonds and pays the spread over its funding cost to forest countries at about $4 per hectare of standing forest a year, with at least 20 percent going to Indigenous peoples and local communities, for countries whose deforestation stays below 0.5 percent a year [@Barber2025]. Each hectare deforested cuts the payment by 100 times the per-hectare rate where deforestation is below 0.3 percent, and by 200 times above it [@Mongabay2025]. Sponsors had pledged $6.7 billion by late November 2025 [@Barber2025]. The TFFF is the first large instrument that pays for the stock. It is also, in effect, interest on a notional value, the first of the four NCV formulations reconciled below, with the leverage on the investment side rather than the guarantee side.

*Payment for environmental services and conservation contracts.* Payments for environmental services work when the payment exceeds the landholder's opportunity cost and is conditional on the service [@Engel2008]. Harstad shows that when a resource owner can sell a stock or its extraction rights, buying conservation directly can beat taxing demand, because the payment changes the owner's outside option rather than the buyer's price [@Harstad2016]. On the fossil side, buying or retiring coal deposits is the supply-side analogue [@Harstad2012], and the case for a supply-side treaty that compensates owners for leaving reserves unexploited has been made on both efficiency and fairness grounds [@CollierVenables2014; @Asheim2019].

*Guarantees and the cost of capital.* The cost of capital for renewable power is several percentage points higher in developing than in advanced economies [@Steffen2020], and that gap alone can lock developing countries into higher-carbon paths [@Ameli2021]. A loan guarantee is a put option on the borrower's assets [@Merton1977]; its value to the borrower is the market's price of that option, while its cost to the guarantor is the guarantor's own expected loss. The two diverge when the guarantor is a preferred creditor. MDB sovereign and sovereign-guaranteed loans defaulted at 0.77 percent a year over 1984–2024, with 95.1 percent recovered [@GEMs2025], an expected loss of about 0.04 percent a year, while the same sovereigns pay market spreads of several hundred basis points. Gabon's 2023 debt-for-nature swap shows the gap: a bond carrying US political risk insurance priced at 6.097 percent and was rated Aa2, fourteen notches above the sovereign, when Gabon's other bonds yielded 9–10.5 percent [@Reuters2023Gabon].

*Clubs and timing.* A climate club works by offering members a benefit that non-members lose [@Nordhaus2015]. Cheaper borrowing is such a benefit, and unlike trade penalties it costs the club little to supply. On timing, the theory of irreversible investment under uncertainty shows that the option to wait raises the hurdle for acting now above the simple net-present-value rule [@DixitPindyck1994]. Falling technology costs make waiting more attractive still, so an incentive that is constant over time is weakest exactly when action is most valuable.

*The gap.* No existing instrument rewards the stock at a scale that matters, prices each tonne at the margin, arrives before the policy cost is paid and costs donors much less than it is worth. Results-based payments price the margin but pay late and against baselines. The TFFF pays for the stock, but at a few dollars per hectare. Guarantees are cheap to supply but are allocated by project and envelope, not by climate performance. This paper joins the three.

# The notional capitalized value {#sec-definition}

## Definition: a balance that the stock opens and emissions draw down

A country's notional capitalized value is a climate balance held for it by an international arrangement. It opens at the value of the country's carbon stock and moves each year with its emissions:

$$B_0 = p_s S_0, \qquad B_{t+1} = B_t + p_e\,(A_t - E_t), \qquad B_t \ge 0.$$ {#eq-balance}

Here $S_0$ is the verified carbon stock at entry in tonnes of CO₂ (forest carbon, and optionally fossil reserves legally retired), $p_s$ is the *stock price* in dollars of opening balance per tonne of stock, $E_t$ is the country's emissions in year $t$ from all sources including land use, $A_t$ is its *allowance*, an agreed benchmark path, and $p_e$ is the *debit price* in dollars per tonne. Emitting above the allowance debits the balance; emitting below it credits the balance. Deforestation enters through $E_t$ as land-use emissions, so the forest stock is not revalued each year; every tonne emitted, from a chimney or a cleared hectare, costs the same $p_e$.

The balance is notional. Nobody claims that Guyana's forests could be sold for $p_s S_0$; the number is an agreed basis for an entitlement [@StrettonTC, ch. 21]. The idea has a mirror image in liability law: an emission inflicts damage on identifiable people in the future, so the prudent response is to provision for it, which makes it a capital requirement rather than an expense [@StrettonRPWT, ch. 7]. The NCV applies the same accounting to the country that holds a stock: an unreleased stock is notional capital, and each tonne released is a withdrawal from it.

The balance sets *guarantee capacity*:

$$G_t = \lambda_t B_t, \qquad X_t = \min(G_t, D_t),$$ {#eq-capacity}

where $\lambda_t$ is the *capacity ratio* (dollars of guarantee capacity per dollar of balance, possibly declining over time), $D_t$ is the country's outstanding eligible green borrowing, and $X_t$ is the exposure actually guaranteed. Utilization $u_t = X_t/G_t$ is the share of capacity in use.

## Four formulations, reconciled

Earlier drafts contain four versions of the idea. @tbl-formulations sets them side by side.

| Version and source | What the country gets | Stock base | Annual adjustment | Role here |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Interest on a notional value (Climate Investment Trust drafts; *Time and Chance* ch. 20) | Interest on, say, a $1tn Amazon valuation, paid into a trust account | Forest; coal in one draft | Not specified | Variant for countries that do not borrow (@sec-delivery) |
| Notional Capitalized Carbon Value (*Time and Chance* ch. 21) | Guarantee capacity released over ten years | Forest, unburned fossil fuel | Minus price × net emissions | Main form, with arithmetic corrected (@sec-ch21) |
| Climate balance on stocks and long-run emissions (research page) | Guarantee support, used up by business-as-usual emissions | Stocks and long-run path | Debited by business-as-usual emissions | Main form; the debit made per tonne |
| Climate allowance of guarantee capacity (DPhil proposal) | Rules-based guarantee capacity adjusted with performance | Not specified | Rises with early action, falls when targets are missed | The release schedule of Proposition 3 |

: Four formulations of the notional capitalized value, and what this paper keeps from each. *Source: the author's earlier drafts [@StrettonTC; @StrettonRPWT; @StrettonDPhil].* {#tbl-formulations}

The four versions agree on the core and differ on three choices, which this paper settles.

*Reward form: guarantee capacity, not interest.* Interest paid into an account is cash, deferred; it costs donors a dollar per dollar of incentive. Guarantee capacity costs a fraction of its value (Proposition 1). It also arrives when a government needs it, as cheaper borrowing for the investments that the policy requires, rather than years after the result. Interest into a trust account remains the right form for countries that do not borrow in volume, such as small island states without bond market access or a country whose oil revenue makes borrowing unnecessary.

*Capacity is a cap on outstanding exposure, not a flow of new guarantees.* The original arithmetic did not say which, and the difference is a factor of ten (@sec-ch21). A cap on outstanding exposure is the natural reading of a balance, matches how MDBs manage guarantee limits, and gives the debit a clean meaning: every dollar debited is a dollar less of exposure the country can have guaranteed from then on.

*The debit is per tonne emitted, against an allowance, at its own price.* "Used up by business-as-usual emissions" could mean a fixed draw-down set by a forecast. That would have no effect on behavior (Proposition 2). The debit must move with actual emissions. Setting the debit price separately from the stock price is the main change from all four drafts, and @sec-model explains why it is needed.

## Why the stock and the debit need different prices

A single price cannot both size the balance and price the margin. Suppose $p_s = p_e = p$. For the debit to bite, capacity must bind: the country must want to use more guarantee capacity than it has, so $\lambda B_t < D_t$. With Guyana's stock of 19.5 billion tonnes and eligible borrowing of, say, $5 billion, a binding balance requires $p < \$0.26$ per tonne, and the marginal tonne is then worth about $0.15 to the country (@sec-forest). At the $100 per tonne of the original proposal, the balance is $1.95 trillion, capacity never binds, and the marginal tonne is worth nothing.

The two prices do different jobs. The stock price decides how much capacity each country starts with, which is a question of distribution and of what the country stands to lose. The debit price decides what each tonne costs, which is the question of incentives. Separating them lets the stock reward large forest countries without paying them for tonnes they were never going to emit, and lets the debit price be set high enough to change behavior without creating a balance no guarantor could stand behind.

The stock still matters at the margin, for a reason the separation makes clear. An international feebate between countries founders on negative transfers, because no sovereign will write a check for exceeding its benchmark; a deduction from a balance held in trust is enforceable where a payment is not [@StrettonRPWT, ch. 5]. The opening balance is what the debit is deducted from. Without a stock there is nothing to debit; with one, a country that emits loses something it already counts as its own.

# Model {#sec-model}

## Setup

A country holds balance $B_t$ under @eq-balance and capacity $G_t$ under @eq-capacity. Guaranteed borrowing pays the guarantor's rate rather than the market rate, saving $\Delta s$ per dollar of guaranteed exposure per year. The guarantor's annual expected loss per dollar of exposure is $\pi L$, the probability of a loss times the loss given default. Behind the guarantees sits a buffer fund holding $k$ dollars of capital per dollar of exposure; holding it costs $\varphi$ a year per dollar, the donors' opportunity cost of funds net of what the buffer earns. The guarantor may charge a fee $f$ per dollar of exposure. Time is discrete in Proposition 1 and continuous in Propositions 2 and 3, with discount rate $r$ and discount factor $\delta = 1/(1+r)$.

The *incentive value* to the country is the present value of spread saved, net of fees:

$$V = \sum_t \delta^t (\Delta s - f) X_t.$$ {#eq-value}

The *cost to the guarantor and donors* is expected loss plus buffer carry, net of fees:

$$C = \sum_t \delta^t (\pi L + k\varphi - f) X_t.$$ {#eq-cost}

## Proposition 1: a guarantee is worth several times what it costs {#sec-p1}

**Proposition 1 (incentive-to-cost ratio).** *If $\Delta s$, $\pi L$, $k$, $\varphi$ and $f$ are constant over the life of the exposure, then for any path of guaranteed exposure*

$$\frac{V}{C} = R \equiv \frac{\Delta s - f}{\pi L + k\varphi - f}.$$ {#eq-ratio}

*A guarantee delivers more incentive per dollar of donor cost than a grant ($R > 1$) if and only if $\Delta s > \pi L + k\varphi$. A fee $f = \pi L + k\varphi$ makes the scheme self-financing while the country keeps $\Delta s - \pi L - k\varphi$ a year per dollar of exposure.*

The proof is in Appendix A. The ratio does not depend on the size or timing of the exposure, so it is the right summary statistic for comparing a guarantee with a grant. A grant of a dollar costs a dollar and is worth a dollar, so $R = 1$.

Why should the spread saved exceed the guarantor's cost? Because the market prices the sovereign's risk to all creditors, while the guarantor bears the sovereign's risk to it. MDBs are preferred creditors and, for guarantees with a sovereign counter-indemnity, hold a claim on the government that governments have strong reasons to honor. Their record bears this out: sovereign and sovereign-guaranteed loans defaulted at 0.77 percent a year over four decades and recovered 95.1 percent [@GEMs2025], an expected loss of 0.038 percent a year. The resource being spent is the gap between the risk the guarantor actually bears and the risk the market charges for [@StrettonTC, ch. 21]. It needs no appropriation, but it is not free: losses will occur, and a buffer must stand behind the exposure.

This paper does not rely on that record. Its base case uses the parameters of the companion paper on the Climate Investment Trust, which sizes the buffer behind the guarantees [@StrettonWP32]: a 3 percent annual probability that a government fails to honor its obligation to the guarantor and a 37 percent loss when it does, the average haircut in sovereign restructurings over 1970–2010 [@CrucesTrebesch2013], for an expected loss of 1.11 percent a year, nearly 30 times the MDB record. A buffer of 9.3 percent of exposure then keeps the annual chance of exhausting it at 1 percent across 20 guaranteed programs with correlation 0.2, so $5 billion of buffer supports about $54 billion of guarantees [@StrettonWP32]. The buffer is invested in safe assets and earns the rate used to discount, so its carry cost is zero ($\varphi = 0$). With $\Delta s$ = 3 percent, $R$ = 3/1.11 = 2.7, the figure the companion paper reports for interest savings per dollar held. If the loss per call is 10 percent rather than 37, $R$ = 10; on the MDB record, about 80. Charging the buffer a 2 percent carry cost lowers the base ratio only to 2.3 (@fig-ratio).

## Proposition 2: the debit must be per tonne, and capacity must bind {#sec-p2}

The marginal incentive is what changes behavior. Let capacity bind on an interval of time, meaning $0 < \lambda_t B_t < D_t$, so every extra dollar of capacity is used and every dollar lost reduces guaranteed exposure. Let the capacity ratio decline at rate $\theta \ge 0$, $\lambda_t = \lambda_0 e^{-\theta t}$.

**Proposition 2 (incentive compatibility and the carbon-price equivalent).**

*(a) If capacity binds from time $s$ onward, a tonne emitted at $s$ costs the country, in present value at $s$,*

$$\tau(s) = \frac{\lambda_0\, p_e\, (\Delta s - f)}{r + \theta}\, e^{-\theta s}.$$ {#eq-cpe}

*This is the carbon-price equivalent of the scheme: the uniform carbon price that gives the same reward for abating one tonne.*

*(b) If the debit is fixed in advance from a forecast of business-as-usual emissions rather than charged per tonne emitted, the marginal incentive is zero.*

*(c) The allowance path $A_t$ does not enter $\tau(s)$. It changes the level of the balance, and so who gains, but not the reward per tonne.*

*(d) If capacity does not bind, because $\lambda_t B_t \ge D_t$ (the country has more capacity than borrowing) or $B_t = 0$ (the balance is exhausted), the marginal incentive in those years is zero.*

The proof is in Appendix A. Part (a) gives the conversion rate from notional to effective price. With no decline in capacity, $\tau = \lambda_0 p_e \Delta s / r$: at a 3 percent spread and a 5 percent discount rate, a dollar of debit price is worth 60 cents of carbon price. The donors' cost per tonne of carbon-price equivalent is $\tau \cdot (\pi L + k\varphi)/\Delta s$, about 37 cents per dollar in the base case. The carbon-price equivalent is the same measure the series uses for every other instrument [@CFPB17], so the NCV can be compared directly with a tax, a feebate or policy crediting.

Part (b) is the reason the debit must be per tonne emitted. A schedule that draws the balance down by business-as-usual emissions whatever the country does is a declining transfer, and a transfer changes nothing at the margin. "Used up by business-as-usual emissions" must mean that business-as-usual emissions would use it up, not that they are assumed to.

Part (c) turns the hardest dispute in results-based finance, the baseline, into a question of distribution. A generous allowance gives a country more balance, but each tonne still costs $p_e$. Negotiators can trade allowance against participation without weakening the incentive, which is not true of crediting against a baseline, where an inflated baseline pays for tonnes that were never at risk.

Part (d) gives two design rules. Capacity must be sized to the country's borrowing, so that it binds; surplus balance above $D_t/\lambda_t$ should flow somewhere it still has value, such as a beneficiary account in the Climate Investment Trust [@CFPB32]. And the allowance must keep the balance positive along a path the country can reach, because a country that expects to exhaust its balance has no incentive in the years after exhaustion and a weaker one before.

## Proposition 3: paying for acting now {#sec-p3}

A government chooses when to adopt a policy, such as a coal-retirement program or a forest-enforcement regime. Adopting at time $T$ costs $K_0 e^{-gT}$ up front, a cost that falls at rate $g$ as technology improves, and cuts emissions by $\Delta E$ tonnes a year from then on. The country values each tonne abated at $b$ (domestic co-benefits, such as cleaner air) and bears an ongoing cost of $\omega$ per tonne (for example, agricultural rent forgone on protected forest). Under the NCV each tonne abated at time $s$ is worth $m(s)$ to the country, the carbon-price equivalent of @eq-cpe, which we write in the general declining form $m(s) = m_\infty + (m_0 - m_\infty)e^{-\theta s}$ with a floor $m_\infty \ge 0$. The net present value of adopting at $T$ is

$$W(T) = \int_T^\infty \Delta E\,[m(s) + b - \omega]\,e^{-rs}\,ds \;-\; K_0 e^{-(r+g)T}.$$ {#eq-w}

**Proposition 3 (early action).** *Suppose the persistence condition $m_\infty + b \ge \omega$ holds and the incentive declines no faster than technology costs, $\theta \le g$. Then acting now ($T = 0$) is optimal if and only if*

$$\Delta E\,(m_0 + b - \omega) \;\ge\; (r + g)\,K_0.$$ {#eq-actnow}

*The minimum initial incentive is $m_0^* = (r+g)K_0/\Delta E + \omega - b$. Holding $m_0 = m_0^*$, the donor cost of the incentive falls as $\theta$ rises, so among schedules satisfying the conditions the cheapest declines at $\theta = g$ toward the floor $m_\infty = \max(\omega - b, 0)$.*

The proof is in Appendix A. The condition has a plain reading. Waiting a year saves interest on the up-front cost ($rK_0$) and lets the cost fall ($gK_0$); acting a year sooner earns a year of net benefit from the abated tonnes. Falling technology costs raise the hurdle: the faster solar or storage costs fall, the more a government gains by waiting, and the bigger the early incentive must be. Without an incentive and with $b < \omega + (r+g)K_0/\Delta E$, the government never acts, because waiting always reduces the loss.

The persistence floor separates two cases. For an energy transition, the ongoing cost of keeping clean capacity is close to zero once it is cheaper than coal, so $\omega \approx 0$ and the incentive can phase out: the reward is needed to start, not to continue. For forests, the opportunity cost of standing forest persists as long as there is land demand, so $\omega > 0$ and the floor stays: a forest needs a permanent price, an energy transition a temporary early one. A single scheme can serve both because the floor and the decay are parameters, not constants.

Uncertainty raises the hurdle further. If the up-front cost follows a random walk, the standard result is that the trigger rises by a factor $\beta/(\beta - 1) > 1$, where $\beta$ depends on volatility and the discount rate [@DixitPindyck1994]. With a 5 percent discount rate, no drift and volatility of 15–20 percent a year, the factor is about 1.6–1.9 (author's calculation). The early-action condition then requires an initial incentive half as large again, or twice as large, as @eq-actnow. The decaying schedule is the instrument for this: a government that knows capacity per tonne falls each year it delays faces a cost of waiting that the market alone does not impose. This is the early-action premium of the series, built into the release schedule.

## Three quantities, kept apart {#sec-quantities}

The framework keeps apart three quantities that discussions of climate finance often merge [@StrettonDPhil]. *Mitigation effectiveness* is $\Delta E$: the emissions cut that a policy produces. *The sovereign incentive required* is $m_0^*$ in @eq-actnow: the reward per tonne that makes acting now worth more than waiting. *The resource cost* to MDBs and donors is $m_0^* (\pi L + k\varphi)/\Delta s$ per tonne: what it costs to create that incentive through guarantees. A grant makes the third quantity equal to the second; a guarantee divides it by $R$.

# Calibration {#sec-calibration}

| Eligible green borrowing (forest country) | $D$ | $5 billion | Stylized |

: Parameters for the calibration. *Note: pp = percentage points. Stylized values are illustrative, not estimates for any country.* {#tbl-params}

The spread saved is the most important input and the most country-specific. Three percentage points is the saving Gabon achieved with insurance on a single bond and the figure used in the original proposal [@StrettonTC, ch. 21]. It applies to a country rated well below investment grade. For an investment-grade sovereign the saving is smaller, perhaps 1–1.5 points, and the case for guarantees weaker; @sec-coal returns to this.

## Correcting the original arithmetic {#sec-ch21}

The original proposal values a forest stock of 100 MtCO₂ at $100 per tonne, a balance of $10 billion, debited by $100 million for each million tonnes emitted. It releases the balance over ten years, "roughly $1 billion of NCCV capacity per year", and, at a saving of 3 percent per dollar guaranteed, finds "$30 million in annual interest-cost reductions" and $300 million over ten years [@StrettonTC, ch. 21]. The text does not say whether the $1 billion is a cap on outstanding exposure or a flow of new guarantees each year. @tbl-ch21 shows that the answer changes the incentive tenfold.

| Reading | Outstanding guaranteed exposure | Annual saving | Total saving | Present value at 5% | Price of a tonne emitted |
|:---|:---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A. $1bn cap on outstanding exposure for 10 years | $1bn | $30m | $0.3bn | $0.23bn | $0 (capacity slack) |
| B. $1bn of new 10-year guarantees each year for 10 years | Rises to $10bn | $30m rising to $300m | $3.0bn over the loans' lives | $1.88bn | Depends on which year's issue is cut |
| C. Whole $10bn balance as a cap from year 1 | $10bn | $300m | $3.0bn over 10 years | $2.32bn | About $21/t with 9 years left |

: Three readings of the original NCCV arithmetic: a fixed $10 billion balance, 3 percent spread saved. *Note: B assumes bullet loans of 10 years. Price of a tonne emitted under C is $100 × 3% × the 9-year annuity factor at 5%. Source: @StrettonTC, ch. 21; author's calculations (Appendix B).* {#tbl-ch21}

The $30 million and $300 million figures are correct only under reading A, and reading A is the worst design. With $1 billion of capacity against a $10 billion balance, capacity does not bind until the country has emitted 90 MtCO₂, so for decades an extra tonne costs nothing (Proposition 2(d)). Under reading C, the natural reading of a balance, the incentive is $300 million a year and each tonne emitted costs about $21 in lost spread savings. The correction does not change the donor cost per dollar of incentive, which is set by Proposition 1; it changes how much incentive a given balance delivers, by a factor of ten.

## A forest country {#sec-forest}

Take a stylized forest country with Guyana's verified stock: 19.5 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent on about 18 million hectares, an average of about 1,080 tonnes per hectare [@Guyana2022LCDS]. Give it $5 billion of eligible green borrowing (stylized), a stock price that opens the balance at that level ($p_s$ = $0.26 per tonne), a debit price of $50 per tonne, and emissions of 15 MtCO₂ a year from all sources against an allowance that falls from 12 Mt in 2027 to zero in 2050 (stylized).

*Incentive and cost.* With capacity fully used, the country saves $150 million a year, $1.87 billion in present value over 20 years. Donors hold a buffer of $0.47 billion and bear an expected annual cost of $56 million. Each tonne emitted costs the country $30 in lost spread savings ($50 × 3% ÷ 5%), and each hectare cleared about $32,500. Donors' cost per tonne of that carbon-price equivalent is about $11, against the $20 per tonne Hess pays in cash for credits against a reference level.

*Business as usual drains the balance; action keeps it.* Under business as usual the debit grows as the allowance falls, and the balance is exhausted in 2042 (@fig-balance). A country that cuts emissions from 15 to 3 Mt by 2037 keeps its balance near or above its borrowing need throughout. The present value of spread savings over 2027–2050 is $2.11 billion if the country acts and $1.13 billion if it does not; acting is worth about $1 billion to it.

![A per-tonne debit drains the balance under business as usual. Stylized forest country: opening balance $5 billion, debit $50 per tonne of CO₂ against an allowance falling from 12 Mt to zero in 2050. Capacity above the $5 billion borrowing line is unused, so in the action case the surplus should flow to a beneficiary account. Source: author's calculations (Appendix B).](2.Source/figures/fig1-balance-paths.png){#fig-balance}

*Comparison with existing instruments.* @tbl-forest puts the scheme beside the Guyana–Hess sale and the TFFF, converting each to a price per tonne at Guyana's average carbon density. The TFFF's $4 per hectare a year is about $0.004 per tonne of stock a year, equivalent to a stock price of $0.07 per tonne capitalized at 5 percent: a reward for the stock at about a quarter of the stock price used here. Its deforestation deduction of $400–800 per hectare is $0.37–0.74 per tonne released. The Hess price of $20 per tonne pays for avoided flow against a reference level and only for the credits sold. The NCV at a $50 debit price gives the stock a balance comparable to the TFFF's capitalized value and prices each tonne released at about 40–80 times the TFFF's deduction.

| Instrument | What is rewarded | Annual value to country | Price of a tonne released |
|:---|:---|:--:|:--:|
| Guyana–Hess ART-TREES sale (2016–2030) | Avoided deforestation below a reference level | About $50m (at least $750m over about 15 years) | $15–20 for credits sold |
| TFFF at $4/ha (Guyana-scale forest) | Standing forest area | About $72m | $0.37–0.74 (deduction per hectare ÷ density) |
| NCV, $5bn capacity, $50 debit (stylized) | Stock (opening balance) and every tonne emitted | $150m in spread saved | About $30 |

: Three ways of rewarding a forest country, at Guyana's carbon density of about 1,080 tCO₂e per hectare. *Note: The TFFF row multiplies $4 by 18 million hectares and assumes full eligibility; payments depend on fund returns. Sources: @GuyanaDPI2023, @Barber2025, @Mongabay2025, @Guyana2022LCDS; author's calculations.* {#tbl-forest}

Two cautions apply. Guyana itself may be an awkward case for a guarantee-based reward: with oil revenue flowing since production began in 2019, its need for guaranteed borrowing may be small relative to its stock, and for such a country the interest-on-balance variant is the better form (@sec-delivery). And average density hides wide variation: a hectare of peat swamp or old-growth forest holds far more than a degraded one, so the debit per hectare cleared should use measured, not average, density.

## How big must the scheme be? {#sec-scale}

The incentive scales with guaranteed borrowing, not with the stock. Proposition 1 makes the arithmetic linear: at a 3 percent saving, each $1 billion a year of incentive needs $33 billion of outstanding guarantee capacity, a 9.3 percent buffer of $3.1 billion, and $370 million a year of expected donor cost (@tbl-scale).

| Incentive to the country | Guarantee capacity needed | Buffer held (9.3%) | Expected donor cost a year | Present value of incentive over 20 years |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $0.1bn a year | $3bn | $0.3bn | $37m | $1.2bn |
| $0.5bn a year | $17bn | $1.6bn | $185m | $6.2bn |
| $1bn a year | $33bn | $3.1bn | $370m | $12.5bn |
| $5bn a year | $167bn | $15.5bn | $1.85bn | $62bn |

: What a big incentive needs, at a 3 percentage point spread saving. *Source: author's calculations (Appendix B), baseline parameters of @tbl-params.* {#tbl-scale}

These numbers explain why the guarantee form matters. The largest sovereign sustainability-linked loan to date, Uruguay's $350 million World Bank loan of 2023, can save the country at most about $12.5 million over its life [@CFPB33]. A results-based payment of $1 billion a year would be among the largest climate transfers ever voted. A guarantee scheme delivering $1 billion a year of spread savings needs donors to hold $3.1 billion, which they keep and which earns, and to accept about $370 million a year of expected losses in the base case, or about $13 million on the MDB record. The buffer is the hard part, and holding it is the job of the Climate Investment Trust [@CFPB32; @StrettonWP32].

The binding constraint is borrowing, not donor money. A country can only save spread on debt it actually issues, so the scheme delivers big incentives to countries that borrow a lot at high spreads: large, lower-rated forest and coal countries. For small or lightly indebted countries, the ceiling on the guarantee form is low, and the interest-on-balance variant or a link to the trust's accounts must carry the reward.

## A coal-reserve country {#sec-coal}

Fossil reserves raise the same question from the supply side: should a country be rewarded for coal it leaves in the ground? Indonesia had 34.9 billion tonnes of proved coal reserves at the end of 2020 [@BP2021], about 78 billion tonnes of CO₂ at IPCC default carbon contents [@IPCC2006]. Valuing the whole reserve even at $1 per tonne would open a balance of $78 billion, and would reward the country for owning coal rather than for keeping it unburned.

Crediting the whole reserve would be a mistake. It rewards the largest fossil holders most, invites countries to report larger reserves, and pays for coal that would never be mined at today's prices. The right base is narrower: credit only reserves that are legally and verifiably retired, by canceling concessions or mining licenses, and debit combustion emissions at the debit price as for any other country. Retiring 2 billion tonnes of bituminous coal, about 4.9 billion tonnes of CO₂, at a stock price of $1 per tonne would open $4.9 billion of capacity.

What that capacity is worth depends on the spread. For an investment-grade sovereign saving 1 percentage point, it is worth $49 million a year and each $1 of debit price converts to only 20 cents of carbon price; at a 3-point saving it would be worth $146 million a year. Guarantees are a strong incentive for countries that borrow at high spreads and a weak one for investment-grade emitters. For the latter, the same balance is better delivered as access to the trust's collateral, or as a reward linked to sustainability-linked lending [@CFPB33].

Supply-side credits also leak. Retiring Indonesian reserves raises the world coal price and draws supply from elsewhere, so the emissions avoided are smaller than the carbon in the reserves retired [@Harstad2012]. The debit on combustion emissions does not leak in this way, because it prices what the country burns. A coal country's reward should therefore come mainly from the debit on its own emissions, with reserve retirement credited at a low stock price to reflect leakage.

## Early action in numbers {#sec-early}

Take a stylized energy reform: retiring coal capacity and replacing it with renewables at a net up-front cost of $1 billion, falling 5 percent a year as technology improves, cutting emissions by 5 MtCO₂ a year, with no domestic co-benefit counted and no ongoing cost. The minimum initial incentive from @eq-actnow is $(0.05 + 0.05) \times \$1\text{bn} / 5\text{ Mt} = \$20$ per tonne; with an option-value multiplier of 1.5 it is $30 per tonne. Below that level the government gains by waiting, and without any incentive it never acts (@fig-timing).

![Below the minimum incentive, delay beats acting now. Net present value of adopting a stylized reform in each year, for incentives at 120 percent, 60 percent and zero of the minimum in @eq-actnow. Reform costs $1 billion up front, falling 5 percent a year, and cuts 5 MtCO₂ a year; the incentive decays at 5 percent a year; discount rate 5 percent. Source: author's calculations (Appendix B).](2.Source/figures/fig3-early-action.png){#fig-timing}

The decaying schedule halves the donor cost. To give $20 per tonne at the start with capacity that does not decline needs a debit price of $33 per tonne and costs donors $740 million in present value. With capacity declining at 5 percent a year, matching the fall in technology costs, the debit price must be $67 per tonne to deliver the same $20 at the start, but donors' present-value cost falls to $370 million, because the incentive is concentrated where it changes the decision. Delivered as cash on results, the same incentive would cost $1 billion.

![A guarantee is worth several times what it costs. Ratio of incentive value to guarantor cost (Proposition 1) against the guarantor's expected loss, for three spread savings. The buffer earns the discount rate, so cost equals expected loss. Dotted lines mark the series base case (3 percent annual calls, 37 percent loss) and a 10 percent loss per call; the MDB sovereign record, 0.04 percent a year, is off the chart. Source: author's calculations; @StrettonWP32; @GEMs2025.](2.Source/figures/fig2-incentive-cost-ratio.png){#fig-ratio}

*Sensitivity.* The ratio of value to cost is most sensitive to the spread saved and the loss per call (@fig-ratio). Halving the spread to 1.5 points halves the ratio to 1.4; cutting the loss per call from 37 to 10 percent, which is plausible if obligations to the guarantor rank with those to MDBs, raises it to 10. The carbon-price equivalent is proportional to the debit price and the spread and inversely proportional to the discount rate plus decay, so a country with a 4.5-point spread gets half as much again per tonne as one with 3 points. None of these changes reverses a conclusion: the guarantee form delivers more incentive per donor dollar than a grant unless expected losses exceed the spread saved, 3 percent a year in the base case, nearly 80 times the MDB record.

# Institutional delivery {#sec-delivery}

*MDBs issue the guarantees; a buffer fund stands behind them.* The guarantees are ordinary MDB instruments: policy-based or project guarantees on the country's eligible green borrowing, with a sovereign counter-indemnity in the IBRD style. The NCV adds a rule for how much capacity each country gets, outside its normal lending envelope. The buffer that absorbs losses before they reach MDB capital is held by a fund that keeps capital rather than spending it; the Climate Investment Trust proposed in the companion paper is that fund [@CFPB32; @StrettonWP32]. Holding capital rather than disbursing it is where the leverage comes from: a buffer sized to stressed losses supports exposure several times its size.

*Eligible borrowing must be defined narrowly.* Capacity should cover borrowing for investments that cut emissions or protect stocks: clean power, grids, forest enforcement and monitoring, and the payment guarantees that make power purchase agreements bankable [@CFPB21]. Guarantee capacity earned under the NCV can stand behind the payment intermediary's waterfall in that paper or the senior bonds of the asset-class structure in its companion [@CFPB22].

*Interest on the balance, into a trust account, is the variant for non-borrowers.* For a country that does not borrow enough for capacity to bind, the arrangement pays interest at rate $i$ on the balance into a beneficiary account in the Climate Investment Trust, pledgeable as collateral now and withdrawable after 2050. The marginal incentive per tonne becomes $p_e\, i/(r+\theta)$ in place of $p_e \Delta s/(r+\theta)$, and the donor cost is the full interest, deferred, rather than a fraction of it. Surplus balance above a borrower's capacity need can flow into the same account, so the debit never goes slack.

*Sustainability-linked lending is the delivery channel for the performance link.* The debit and the allowance can be written as key performance indicators in a sustainability-linked loan or bond, so that meeting the allowance path both preserves the balance and triggers a step-down in the loan's margin. Codified indicators and verification make that link routine [@CFPB33].

*Verification uses existing systems.* Forest stocks and land-use emissions can be measured under jurisdictional standards such as ART-TREES, which already issue credits at national scale; fossil emissions come from national inventories under the Paris transparency framework. The NCV needs these measurements annually, not a new market.

# Risks and safeguards {#sec-risks}

*Moral hazard: the guarantee makes the country borrow more.* Cheaper borrowing invites more borrowing, and a guaranteed creditor has less reason to discipline the sovereign. Three features limit this. Capacity is capped by the balance, so the exposure is bounded. Only eligible green borrowing is covered. And the sovereign counter-indemnifies the guarantor, so a call on the guarantee becomes a debt to an MDB that the country has strong reasons to repay. The safeguard fails if eligibility is defined loosely or if the counter-indemnity is waived for the weakest borrowers, which is precisely where the spread saved is largest.

*Hidden fiscal exposure.* The scheme does not remove the host government's liabilities. It converts part of its market debt into debt guaranteed by an MDB and backed by the government's own counter-indemnity: the exposure becomes smaller in expected cost, contingent and contracted, but it is still the government's. On the donor side, guarantee exposure is a contingent liability that capital-adequacy rules must count. A buffer sized to expected loss alone is used but not used up in normal years and is exhausted in a correlated crisis [@StrettonTC, ch. 14]; the buffer must be sized to stressed losses and its size published.

*Valuation disputes.* Countries will contest stock measurements, densities, allowances and the price. Separating the two prices narrows the stakes. Disputes over the stock and the allowance affect only the level of the balance, which is a matter of distribution and can be settled by negotiation (Proposition 2(c)). The debit price, which governs incentives, should be uniform across countries and set by rule. Prioritizing forests near ecological thresholds, where losing more forest could trigger dieback of much of the remainder [@LovejoyNobre2018], is better done through a higher debit per hectare in designated zones than through a higher stock value, because the purpose is to price the next hectare cleared, not the hectares already standing.

*Permanence and leakage.* A forest can burn or be cleared after a contract ends. The NCV handles reversal by construction: a tonne released is debited whenever it is released, so a country cannot bank a reward and then reverse. Natural disturbance needs a rule, such as a pooled insurance reserve, so that a fire beyond the government's control does not wipe out a balance. Leakage within a country is avoided by national accounting; leakage across borders, as deforestation or coal supply moves to non-participants, is limited only by broad participation, which is an argument for opening the scheme to all forest and coal countries at once, as the TFFF does for 74 forest countries [@Barber2025].

*Fairness to low-stock countries.* A stock-based balance gives most to countries with large forests and nothing to the Sahel or small island states. This is partly the point, since stocks are what a flow-based scheme fails to reward, but it cannot be the whole design. The allowance is the corrective: a low-emitting country with little stock earns balance every year it emits below its allowance, at the same debit price. A per-capita floor on the opening balance would add a further corrective. Because the incentive scales with borrowing, low-stock, low-borrowing countries are better served by the interest-on-balance variant than by guarantees.

*The strongest objection: this pays for stocks that were never at risk.* Much of Guyana's or the Congo Basin's forest is remote and would stand without any payment, so the opening balance is in large part a transfer for nothing. The answer has three parts. First, the transfer is infra-marginal by design, and it is cheap: what the country receives is capacity, costed to donors at expected loss plus buffer carry, not cash. Second, the opening balance is what makes the per-tonne debit enforceable; without a balance to lose, a sovereign cannot be charged for emitting. Third, by Proposition 2 the incentive at the margin is set by the debit price, not by the opening balance, so a generous stock credit does not dilute the incentive. The objection is right that the stock price should be low. It is wrong that the stock should not be rewarded at all.

# Policy implications {#sec-policy}

MDB shareholders should create a rules-based guarantee capacity outside country lending envelopes, allocated by notional capitalized value. Each participating country would receive an opening balance from its verified carbon stock at a low, uniform stock price, an allowance path to net zero, and a uniform debit price of $30–70 per tonne for emissions above the allowance. Capacity should be sized so that it binds on each country's eligible green borrowing, decline at roughly the rate that clean technology costs fall, and flow any surplus into a beneficiary account.

Donors should fund the buffer rather than the reward. The first-loss buffer behind the guarantees should be held in a trust that invests it, sized to stressed losses on the exposure and published. On the calibration here, a scheme delivering $1 billion a year of incentive needs a buffer of about $3.1 billion and costs about $370 million a year in expected losses in the conservative base case.

Forest and coal countries should negotiate allowances, not baselines. Under the NCV the allowance affects how much a country gets, not how strongly it is rewarded per tonne, so it is a safer object of negotiation than a crediting baseline. Coal countries should seek credit for legally retired reserves at a low stock price, and should expect most of their reward to come from the debit on combustion emissions.

The scheme fails under four conditions. It fails if spreads saved are small, as for investment-grade sovereigns, unless the reward is delivered through the trust's accounts instead. It fails if capacity is set so large that it never binds, which is the trap in the original proposal's release schedule. It fails if the buffer is sized to expected rather than stressed losses, so that a correlated crisis reaches MDB capital. And it fails if verification is captured, so that measured emissions stop tracking real ones.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

A notional capitalized value lets the international system reward what countries have kept as well as what they cut, at a fraction of the cost of paying for either in cash. Two results do most of the work. A guarantee saves the borrower the full spread and costs the provider only its expected loss and the carry on a buffer, so each donor dollar delivers about 2.7 dollars of incentive in a conservative base case and far more on the MDBs' sovereign record. And the stock and the margin need different prices: the stock opens the balance from which each tonne is debited, and the debit price, converted at the spread over the discount rate, sets the carbon-price equivalent. The main limitation is that the incentive scales with what a country borrows and the spread it saves, so the guarantee form is strong for large, lower-rated emitters and forest countries and weak for investment-grade or lightly indebted ones. The next step is to estimate spreads saved and eligible borrowing country by country, and to test with the companion trust model how large a buffer stressed, correlated losses require.

# Appendix A: Proofs {.appendix .unnumbered #sec-appA}

**Proof of Proposition 1.** With constant parameters, @eq-value and @eq-cost give $V = (\Delta s - f)\sum_t \delta^t X_t$ and $C = (\pi L + k\varphi - f)\sum_t \delta^t X_t$. The common factor $\sum_t \delta^t X_t > 0$ cancels, giving @eq-ratio. $R > 1$ if and only if $\Delta s - f > \pi L + k\varphi - f$, that is $\Delta s > \pi L + k\varphi$, provided $\pi L + k\varphi - f > 0$. With $f = \pi L + k\varphi$, $C = 0$ and $V = (\Delta s - \pi L - k\varphi)\sum_t \delta^t X_t$. $\square$

**Proof of Proposition 2.** (a) In continuous time, $\dot B_t = p_e(A_t - E_t)$, so emitting one extra tonne at $s$ lowers $B_t$ by $p_e$ for all $t > s$ (until the balance hits zero). Where capacity binds, $X_t = \lambda_t B_t$, so guaranteed exposure falls by $\lambda_t p_e$ and the country loses $(\Delta s - f)\lambda_t p_e$ a year. The present value at $s$ is
$$\int_s^\infty (\Delta s - f)\, p_e\, \lambda_0 e^{-\theta t} e^{-r(t-s)}\,dt = \frac{\lambda_0 p_e (\Delta s - f)}{r+\theta} e^{-\theta s}.$$
(b) If the debit is $p_e(A_t - \hat E_t)$ with $\hat E_t$ a forecast fixed in advance, $B_t$ does not depend on actual $E_t$, so $\partial V/\partial E_s = 0$. (c) $A_t$ enters $B_t$ additively and does not depend on $E_s$, so $\partial^2 B_t/\partial A\,\partial E_s = 0$ and $\tau(s)$ is unchanged. (d) If $\lambda_t B_t \ge D_t$, then $X_t = D_t$ is locally unaffected by a small change in $B_t$; if $B_t = 0$, the floor in @eq-balance makes $B_t$ locally insensitive to further emissions. In either case the integrand is zero for those $t$. $\square$

**Proof of Proposition 3.** Differentiate @eq-w: $W'(T) = -\Delta E\,[m(T) + b - \omega]e^{-rT} + (r+g)K_0 e^{-(r+g)T}$. Multiply by $e^{(r+g)T} > 0$: the sign of $W'(T)$ is the sign of $h(T) \equiv (r+g)K_0 - \Delta E\,n(T)e^{gT}$, where $n(T) = m(T) + b - \omega = (m_\infty + b - \omega) + (m_0 - m_\infty)e^{-\theta T}$. Then $n(T)e^{gT} = (m_\infty + b - \omega)e^{gT} + (m_0 - m_\infty)e^{(g-\theta)T}$. The first term is non-decreasing because $m_\infty + b - \omega \ge 0$ (persistence), and the second is non-decreasing because $\theta \le g$ and $m_0 \ge m_\infty$. So $h(T)$ is non-increasing. If @eq-actnow holds, $h(0) \le 0$, so $h(T) \le 0$ and $W'(T) \le 0$ for all $T \ge 0$: $W$ is non-increasing and $T = 0$ is optimal. Since $W(T) \to 0$ as $T \to \infty$, also $W(0) \ge 0$, so acting now beats never acting. Conversely, if @eq-actnow fails, $h(0) > 0$, so $W'(0) > 0$ and adopting slightly later beats adopting now.

For the cost result, the donors' present-value cost of incentives for abatement $\Delta E$ from $T = 0$ is $\frac{\pi L + k\varphi}{\Delta s}\int_0^\infty \Delta E\,m(s)e^{-rs}\,ds = \frac{\pi L + k\varphi}{\Delta s}\Delta E\left[\frac{m_\infty}{r} + \frac{m_0 - m_\infty}{r+\theta}\right]$, which is decreasing in $\theta$ for $m_0 > m_\infty$. Under the sufficient condition $\theta \le g$, the cost is minimized at $\theta = g$, with $m_0 = m_0^*$ and $m_\infty$ at its lowest permitted value $\max(\omega - b, 0)$. $\square$

*Remark.* For $\theta > g$, @eq-actnow remains necessary but is no longer sufficient: $h(T)$ may rise and then fall, and a later adoption date can dominate. The code in Appendix B checks $W(T)$ numerically for any schedule.

# Appendix B: Data and code {.appendix .unnumbered #sec-appB}

All calculations are in `2.Source/model.py`, which prints every number used in the paper and the brief; `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py` draws the three figures. Both run with Python 3, NumPy and Matplotlib.

*Anchored data.* Guyana's forest carbon stock (19.5 GtCO₂e) and forest area (about 18 million hectares) are from @Guyana2022LCDS. The Hess sale terms are from @GuyanaDPI2023, and the ART issuance from @OilNow2022. TFFF design figures are from @Barber2025 and the deduction rules from @Mongabay2025, which reports the facility's concept note; the official concept note should be checked before formal publication. The base-case loss and buffer parameters are those of @StrettonWP32, with the loss per call from @CrucesTrebesch2013. The MDB default and recovery rates are from @GEMs2025, the IBRD equity-to-loans minimum from @IBRD2026, and the Gabon bond terms from @Reuters2023Gabon. Indonesia's coal reserves are from @BP2021; carbon contents use IPCC default net calorific values and emission factors for other bituminous coal (25.8 GJ/t, 94.6 kgCO₂/GJ, so 2.44 tCO₂/t) and sub-bituminous coal (18.9 GJ/t, 96.1 kgCO₂/GJ, so 1.82 tCO₂/t), the latter applied to lignite as well, which overstates its carbon [@IPCC2006].

*Stylized inputs.* Eligible green borrowing ($5 billion), the emissions and allowance paths, the debit price ($50 per tonne), the series base case for guarantee losses and buffer size (from the companion paper), the discount rate (5 percent) and the early-action reform (cost $1 billion falling 5 percent a year, 5 MtCO₂ a year cut) are assumptions for illustration.
